Twain
TWAYN
n. or adj. (archaic for two)
Old English twægen, the masculine form of two; survived in modern English only in a few stylized phrases (never the twain shall meet) and in the KJV.

Biblical Definition

Twain is the KJV’s archaic word for two, particularly in contexts of pairs that constitute a unity or that come together in unique theological union. The most theologically weighty use is in Christ’s teaching on marriage, citing Genesis 2: have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh? Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder (Matt 19:4-6). Christ’s use of twain at the marriage-doctrine’s heart is structurally significant. The marriage of one man and one woman creates a new unity such that they are no more twain, but one flesh: the two have become one in a covenantal union grounded in creation itself and not to be undone by human action. The Greek duo behind twain here is the ordinary number-word, but the older English word carries a slight archaic dignity that suits the gravity of the marriage-doctrine. Paul applies the same Genesis 2 text to the deeper mystery of Christ and the church in Ephesians 5:31: for this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh. Other notable KJV uses of twain include the veil of the temple rent in twain from the top to the bottom at the moment of Christ’s death (Matt 27:51), and several proverbial uses (let thine arrows be twain in 2 Kgs 9:24, etc.). The verb’s most enduring application is the marriage-and-union picture: the twain becoming one flesh, no longer twain but one—a creation-grounded unity that human action does not have authority to dissolve. The recovery of the older word is small; the recovery of the underlying doctrine is large: the marriage of one man and one woman creates a one-flesh union that human dissolution does not have authority over, and the saint receives the marriage-covenant as a creation-ordinance with the gravity Christ Himself assigned to it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TWAIN as two; in scripture, used by Christ in His marriage-teaching (they twain shall be one flesh, Matt 19:5) and at the rending of the temple veil at the crucifixion (Matt 27:51).

TWAIN, n. — Two. They twain shall be one flesh (Matt 19:5). The veil of the temple was rent in twain (Matt 27:51).

TWO, n. — One and one; the second cardinal number; a couple; a pair.

Key Scripture

Matthew 19:5-6 — "And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh? Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."

Matthew 27:51 — "And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent."

Genesis 2:24 — "Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh."

Ephesians 5:31-32 — "For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church."

Modern Corruption

Twain is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by its near-disappearance from modern English; more pressingly, the doctrine the word supports—the creation-grounded one-flesh union of one man and one woman in marriage—is corrupted by the present age’s redefinition of marriage and the wholesale denial of the creation-ordinance Christ’s use of twain rests upon.

expand to see more

Twain has dropped from modern English usage almost entirely. The vocabulary loss is small; but the doctrine the word supports—Christ’s teaching on marriage as the one-flesh union of one man and one woman—has come under sustained cultural assault in the present age. Where Christ said they twain shall be one flesh, wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh; what therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder, the present age claims authority to redefine the categories Christ Himself names: twain in marriage need not be one man and one woman; the joining is not God-grounded but socially constructed; the dissolution is at the parties’ discretion; the one-flesh union has no creation-grounding to preserve. The recovery is the recovery of Christ’s appeal to Genesis 2 as the controlling text on marriage: God made them male and female; for this cause a man cleaves to his wife; they twain are one flesh; God has joined; let no man put asunder. Each clause stands; the structure stands; and the redefinitions and dissolutions of the present age fall against the wall of Christ’s own teaching.

Beyond the marriage-doctrine, twain’s other great biblical use is at the moment of Christ’s death: the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom. The twain there is the literal two pieces into which the temple veil split; but the theological significance is that the access between the holy place and the holiest of all, kept closed throughout the Old Testament administration, has been opened by Christ’s atoning death. The torn veil is the architectural confession of the gospel: the way into the holiest is now made manifest, and the saints have boldness to enter by the blood of Jesus (Heb 10:19-22). Rent in twain from the top to the bottom—the older word again carries antique gravity to the moment; the modern torn in two conveys the fact but flattens the register. The KJV vocabulary, retained where it is doing rhetorical work, is part of the dignity with which the English Bible has, for four centuries, set forth the great doctrines of the faith.

Hebrew Roots

Old English twægen (two, masculine form); renders Greek duo (two)—a number-word whose older English form carries antique dignity, especially in Christ’s marriage-teaching (they twain shall be one flesh) and at the rending of the temple veil at the crucifixion.

expand to see more

Old English twægen — two (masculine form; the etymological root).

Greek duo (G1417) — two (the cardinal number).

Hebrew sh’nayim (H8147) — two (the OT cardinal).

Greek dichotomē (G1371) — cutting in two (the related verb behind cut asunder).

Usage

"They twain shall be one flesh; wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh—Christ’s marriage-teaching grounds the union in creation and forbids human dissolution."

"The veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom—the architectural confession at Christ’s death that the way into the holiest is now open."

"Modern two conveys the number; the older twain carries antique dignity that suits the gravity of marriage-doctrine and the moment of the veil’s rending."
